title: Ìjàpá and the Feast Above the Clouds
summary: Ìjàpá the tortoise borrows a feather from every bird to attend a feast in the sky, and learns that a borrowed kindness comes with a price.
moral: A feast eaten alone leaves a shell cracked where all can see.
attribution: A traditional Yoruba tale, retold for Ubuntu Tales.

cover.alt: A flock of birds rising in a dark V above a tortoise whose shell shows a bright crack

sentences.text: There was once a feast in the sky, and every bird in the world was invited.
The tortoise Ìjàpá heard about it from the parrot, who could not keep a secret unless it was told he had no wings at all.
“Take me with you,” Ìjàpá said.
“I have no wings, but I have a very good name, and a very good name is worth more than a pair of wings at a party.”
The parrot looked at the tortoise’s round back and sighed.
“I will ask the others,” he said.
“But you must not eat before speaking, or you will spoil your name.”
The birds each lent Ìjàpá one feather.
They tucked them into the edges of his shell until he was a strange, heavy bird.
He looked at his new wings in a puddle and liked them very much.
He gave each bird a name to remember him by, which is how the birds got the names they still use for one another.
They flew up, higher and higher, until the ground below looked like a cloth laid out for washing.
Ìjàpá held on.
He did not look down, and he did not look up, and he did not say a single word, which was difficult for him.
At the feast in the sky, the food was poured into calabash bowls.
The birds gathered round.
But Ìjàpá had brought a stool and a little bag of chalk, and he gave each bird a chalk mark on the ground.
“You must not begin,” he said, “until the one who has no wings gives the blessing.
It is the custom of my people.”
The birds waited politely.
The food smelled of palm oil and pepper and smoke, and the smell reached down into Ìjàpá’s round belly and made a noise there.
He blessed the food, and then, because the blessing was in his mouth, he ate first.
He ate first and second and third.
He ate as though he had been empty since the world was made.
The birds watched.
They watched until Ìjàpá began to leak, as tortoises do when they have eaten too much.
Then they were no longer polite.
They went to every bird and took back the feather that had been lent, and the parrot, who had arranged the whole thing, took his back last and took it slowly.
Ìjàpá looked at himself: round, heavy, and without a single wing.
“Then I shall tell the sky people a story,” he said, “and they will give me a second feast while you go home.”
But the sky people had already heard the birds, and they were not pleased.
The birds flew home and left Ìjàpá alone in the clouds.
They flew in a long dark line across the evening, and not one of them looked back.
The sky people shut their doors.
The feast was over, and the bowls were being washed, and there was no one left in the sky who wanted to hear a story from a tortoise with no feathers.
The parrot felt sorry for him and swooped back.
“I cannot carry you,” he said, “but I can soften the ground for you.”
So he flew to Ìjàpá’s wife and told her to pile up every soft thing in the house under the place where her husband would fall: the cushions, the mats, the cloths, the cotton.
Some of it was soft.
Much of it was not.
Ìjàpá fell and fell, and when he struck the ground his beautiful shell split into more pieces than a market trader could count.
He lay there for a long time, hummocked and gaping.
His wife came running with a needle and thread, and she sewed the shell back together while the neighbours gathered to look.
She sewed well, but she could not find the piece that had held the middle of his back, so his shell has been cracked and ribbed ever since.
That is why the tortoise never comes to a feast empty-handed, and never goes anywhere he cannot leave on his own feet.
And that is why people say: a feast eaten alone leaves a shell cracked where all can see.
